The building block

The virtual campus: one team, three auto-routed queues

Campus queue

On-site at the hub. Deskside fixes, installs and moves, staging and depot for the whole campus, anchored at the site the demand itself selects.

Local queue

Same day on the road. Sites within drive range of the hub get scheduled and same-day visits from the same team.

Remote queue

Owns the rest of the estate. Every remote site is assigned here, resolved remotely, with OEM or vetted smart hands and shipping when hands are needed.

Tickets route automatically to the right queue by site and work type. Every technician can work any queue, so the team flexes to demand and backs each other up.

One team owns a hub, its drive-range sites, and its remote tail.

Hubs and depots

How the campuses split, and where to sharpen

41% on-site hands
59% remote + shipping

11 Hubs . on-site led

Anchor dense metros with same-day hands; the hub anchors a dense cluster with same-day hands.

18 Depots . remote + shipping led

Incident-versus-remote resolution, dispatch and parts shipping across a long tail; the hub is mainly a staging and coordination point.

A refinement to weigh together

Two hub-led campuses, Mumbai and Paris, also carry a heavy remote tail. Shifting that remote to a sibling depot, since India and France already run several campuses, would let them run as a near-pure hub with a sharper local promise. It trades a little shared capacity, so it is a service-quality call rather than a saving, and the integrated one-team model remains the default.

The shift

A cost shift, not just a labor reduction

Every step up the ratio ladder trades hands-on labor for logistics. Naming that trade up front is what makes the road map credible.

What goes up

Shipping and logistics

More parts and whole devices move by courier instead of by hand; depot staging, imaging and refresh throughput grows.

Dispatch and OEM warranty

Visits beyond drive range go to vetted smart hands and OEM on-site warranty. Dell's OEM warranty model is the strongest expression of this, break-fix lands on the manufacturer, not on headcount.

What offsets it

Remote-first resolution

A remote fix replaces a visit entirely; the three-queue routing keeps pushing work to the cheapest channel that solves it.

Consolidated stock, tighter control

Fewer, better-run stock points replace scattered site closets: less duplication, less loss, real asset visibility, and paid hours that track demand.

The end state is zero-touch. With Intune fully realized (Autopilot enrollment) and Dell's global Life Cycle Hub, devices ship factory-configured from off-site depots directly to the user, with extended factory-grade support behind them. A new install or a refresh needs no technician at all, just shipping.

Labor shifts to logistics; controls and remote-first make the shift a net win.

18
The journey

The real transformation is how users ask for help

Today, many users have a technician within walking distance, so requests flow to the nearest person rather than to the service desk or self-service. That habit, not the org chart, is what this transformation changes, and it changes gradually.

1 Stabilize

Stand up the campuses. Named teams keep local trust, service levels hold, and nothing is taken away on day one. On-site presence stays where the demand is.

2 Shift

Walk-ups route into the three queues. Service-desk-first and self-service habits build with communication and quick wins, and channel mix is measured monthly.

3 Optimize

The model re-derives on live data, real time on task and ticket types. Teams resize by rule, not by cuts, and the ratio rises as reliance on walk-up support falls.

Why 114 is the right starting number: it is deliberately conservative, enough presence to hold service steady while habits shift, and sized to step down by rule as adoption grows. Expectation management and communication are the heart of the plan.

Hold service steady. Shift the habit. Let the data step the model down.

Assumptions

The basis behind every number, and how to refine it

Working calendar

252 working days a year

Demand

87,163 tickets, converted to a daily rate per site

Drive radius

about 60 minutes separates local from remote coverage

On-site throughput

about 6 incidents + 4 requests / tech / day, 50:50 modeled mix

Remote throughput

about 5 / day for triage, remote fix and dispatch coordination

Utilization and floors

85% utilization for travel and escalation; minimum 2 per campus with a low-volume single-tech exception

How we refine it: the role mix and the 50:50 split are modeled on the data we have today. Your addresses and seat counts are now in the model; with role-level ticket volumes we fine-tune the mix and the team size per campus.

The upside

Why this is a stronger operating model

Resilience by design

Pooled, cross-trained teams absorb a spike at any one site from within, instead of overwhelming a lone technician.

Work finds the right hands

Three auto-routed queues send each ticket to the right skill and the right place, with no manual triage.

Build inside the team

Hands-on device work is a named build role drawn from each pool, not a bolt-on cost for every site.

Scales with your estate

The model re-derives from data as Reference Deal A adds or sheds sites: campuses promote or fold automatically, as Peru just demonstrated.

Making it real

What we need from Reference Deal A

1 Close the address gaps

The address extract is missing 60 sites that carry demand, among them the DR Congo, Oman, Zimbabwe and Algeria estates, and 30 sites remain placed at country level. Completing these pulls more sites into same-day local coverage.

2 Ticket split by type

Incident versus service request per site is the one modeled assumption left. Your addresses and seat counts are in; the real work mix is what now changes technician counts directly.

3 Stand up Lima, confirm reach

Validate the new Peru campus, the coverage pairings for Sri Lanka, Iceland and the Dominican Republic, and any flagship sites where you want a larger on-site presence.

4 Phase the rollout

Stand the model up region by region against agreed service levels, starting where the data is strongest, and refine as live volumes land.
